sentences.text: I poured the rest down the sink at two in the morning and stood there until the smell was gone. Day two, and the coffee tastes the way it did in the first ninety, bitter and necessary and endless. Her voicemail said call anytime, so I did, at 3 a.m., shaking, and she picked up like it was noon. Relapse is part of some stories, my counselor says, but she also made me schedule three extra sessions this month. Four years of chips in a drawer, and this morning a plastic white one in my pocket like a stone. Everyone at the eight o'clock group already knew before I opened my mouth; small rooms carry news fast. When I said "one day" instead of "three years," the room just nodded, and somehow that was worse and better at once. My sponsor answered on the second ring, and the first thing she said was that she was glad I called. Maybe the slip doesn't erase the three years; maybe it just proves I can't ever coast on them. How do I tell my daughter the chip on her dresser doesn't mean what it meant last week? Nobody clapped when I took the newcomer chip this time, and I was grateful for the quiet. What I keep replaying is the moment in the parking lot when I still could have driven home. At the podium I couldn't get past my name for a while, and nobody rushed me. She didn't yell; she just moved her car keys back to her purse, the way she used to. Trust, I'm learning, rebuilds on a schedule I don't control — her timeline, not mine, and rightly so. One slip, and now my wife checks the odometer again, quietly, thinking I don't notice. There's a difference between shame and accountability; the meeting keeps teaching me which one actually keeps people sober. The app asked if I was sure before resetting my counter to zero, and I sat with my thumb hovering for a long time. Hardest call of the day wasn't my sponsor; it was my brother, who had only just started trusting me again. Walking back into the Thursday meeting felt like standing under fluorescent lights with my whole year written on my face. That last paragraph took longer than the first ten pages; endings this dark refuse to be rushed. Marisol flagged the ending as too abrupt; she wanted one more beat of silence before the last line. I want to write a suicide letter.
